summary: A 1979 paper describing a datagram-based query and response service for host names and addresses, provided by the ARPANET Network Information Center. It was a new way to distribute and update host name and address information.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 756 describes a service that answers requests for host names and addresses instead of requiring every computer to keep a complete, current list. It also explores possible ways to broaden queries and distribute the service.

questions: how did early networks look up host addresses
what is the nic name server
how did the nic name server answer queries
subtitle: A datagram-based service for looking up host addresses on demand.

tldr.problem: Bulk copies of a network's host database can be incomplete or out of date, especially on hosts with limited memory or infrequent updates.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a datagram query to a name server, which returns an address, similar names when a unique match is unavailable, or an error.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes a provisional centralized NIC service and discusses possible extensions and ways to distribute the service.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 756's status as Unknown. The RFC describes a provisional service and identifies further implementation and design work as ongoing.

sections.title: Why Ask a Name Server
sections.content:
The ARPANET Network Information Center maintained a database of host addresses and distributed copies to hosts. Bulk copies worked for many systems, but some hosts kept incomplete or stale data because memory and update processing were limited.

The RFC presents a transaction-based query and response service as another way to obtain host-address information. A client can ask when it needs an address rather than relying only on a local copy.
sections.plainLanguage: A local host list can be missing entries or updates. A query lets a computer ask a name server for information when it needs it.

sections.title: The Provisional NIC Service
sections.content:
The service described in the RFC ran on SRI-KA, an ARPANET DEC-10, and used the Internet Name Server protocol over the Internet Protocol. The information came from the NIC host-address database, supplied to the server as an input file.

A query could return a host address. For example, the paper shows a query for FOO-TENEX returning the address fields 10 2 0 9. The paper also describes a user querying from a packet-radio terminal and then using the returned address to open a Telnet connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A client sends a name query and receives an address or an error. The paper describes a provisional NIC service whose answers came from the NIC host database.

sections.title: Proposed Query Extensions
sections.content:
The basic service binds a host name to an address. The RFC discusses possible additions, including responses with similar names, query fields for local or all networks, wildcard searches, and queries for service addresses.

These additions are proposals and design questions in the paper, not all features of the basic service. It also considers replies larger than one datagram, dynamic database updates, and architectures that could split or distribute the service.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper suggests ways a future name service could answer broader questions, such as finding a service or matching several names. It presents these as extensions to consider.
